# Regularization and Geometry Constraints

Also called: Regularization, Geometric Priors, Depth Regularization, Frequency Regularization

## Overview
Regularization and geometry constraints augment the standard photometric loss in 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) to enforce structural coherence, prevent overfitting, and resolve ambiguities inherent in sparse-view or unposed reconstruction. Unlike [Base 3DGS Optimization](7549-base-3dgs-optimization.md), which relies solely on pixel-wise color differences, this family introduces explicit penalties on frequency content, depth consistency, or spatial smoothness to guide the optimization of Gaussian primitives toward physically plausible surfaces and sharp details.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family compute a differentiable auxiliary loss term $\mathcal{L}_{reg}$ that is added to the total training loss:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{rgb} + \lambda_{reg} \mathcal{L}_{reg} $$
where $\lambda_{reg}$ is a scalar weight. The core mechanism involves extracting a geometric or spectral property from the rendered output (or the input data) and comparing it against a target or constraint. The gradients of $\mathcal{L}_{reg}$ flow back through the differentiable rasterizer to update the Gaussian parameters $\theta$ (centers $\mu$, scales $s$, rotations $q$, opacities $\alpha$, and colors $c$).

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md)
[Frequency regularization](#6130-frequency-regularization.md) guides optimization by penalizing discrepancies in specific frequency bands of the rendered image. It solves the problem where standard [splatting](#23-splatting.md) methods converge to low-frequency solutions, resulting in blurry details. Unlike [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md), which enforces geometric consistency via depth maps, frequency regularization operates directly on the image or feature space to enforce sharpness. See [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) for implementation details.

### [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md)
[Smoothed 2D supervision](#7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) stabilizes the joint optimization of camera poses and 3D radiance fields by blurring 2D training images with scheduled Gaussian kernels. It produces smoothed image gradients to stabilize camera alignment and restricts the spectrum of the learned scene. It differs from [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) by applying explicit spatial smoothing to the target supervision images rather than penalizing frequency-domain discrepancies in the loss. See [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) for implementation details.

### [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md)
[Depth regularization](#7616-depth-regularization.md) augments the standard photometric loss with terms that enforce geometric consistency between rendered depth maps and external depth estimates (e.g., monocular predictions or stereo disparities). It solves the ambiguity of scale and structure in sparse-view or unposed reconstruction by anchoring Gaussian primitives to explicit surface geometry. It sets itself apart from [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) by operating on spatial depth structures rather than spectral frequency bands, and from [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) by explicitly modeling the depth accumulation process rather than smoothing image-space features. See [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md) for implementation details.

### [3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization](9150-3d-half-gaussian-splatting-covariance-transformation-and-reg.md)
See [3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization](9150-3d-half-gaussian-splatting-covariance-transformation-and-reg.md).

### [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md)
A regularization strategy that constrains 3D Gaussian geometry by encouraging spatial reshaping (movement of centers) rather than deforming Gaussian shapes, preventing detail loss and blurred appearance caused by forcing anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth.

#### Wild-GS
A method that aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes directly to 3D Gaussians and uses depth regularization and visibility maps to mitigate transient effects and constrain geometry [S1].

#### Source Feature Extrapolation
A technique to improve extrapolation capabilities beyond source view frustums by padding source images and adding [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) channels for padded regions, preventing smearing artifacts in regions not visible by source images [S2].
- Apply border padding to source images $I^{(i)}$ [S2].
- Create a channel $\Gamma$ containing pixel-wise positional encodings for padded regions: $\Gamma[u,v] = \gamma(u,v)$ if $(u,v)$ is not in $I^{(i)}$, else 0. Concatenate $I_{pad}$ and $\Gamma$ to form $I'(i) = \text{concatenate}(I_{pad}, \Gamma)$ [S2].
- $\gamma(\cdot)$ denotes positional encoding with exponential frequencies [S2].

#### SDF-Regularized 3DGS
Methods to improve geometric fidelity in 3DGS by imposing physical constraints, such as [Signed Distance Fields](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) (SDFs), monocular depth priors, or multi-view geometric constraints, during optimization [S3].
- Introduce a regularization term to minimize the difference between an ideal SDF and the SDF calculated from Gaussians [S3].
- Use a dual-branch framework with GS- and SDF-branches, jointly optimized to provide mutual guidance [S3].
- Incorporate [geometric regularization](#4970-geometric-and-normal-alignment-losses.md) such as monocular depth priors or multi-plane Gaussian optimization [S3].

#### FreGS
Applies progressive frequency regularization to primitives to prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training [S4, unofficial].

## Background
Original 3D Gaussian Splatting optimizes for photometric loss, often resulting in unstructured density clouds that do not represent a valid surface [S3]. To recover high-quality geometry, recent methods impose physical constraints during optimization [S3]. This can be achieved by integrating Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) into the 3DGS framework [S3]. Alternatively, higher geometrical precision can be obtained by using a dual-branch framework with GS- and SDF-branches, jointly optimized to provide mutual guidance [S3]. Other methods propose to incorporate geometric regularization, such as monocular depth priors [S3]. However, strict depth constraints may lead to incorrect shifts in Gaussian positions [S3].

To prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training, FreGS [S4, unofficial] applies progressive frequency regularization to the primitives. Faster-GS [S4, unofficial] finds that gradient updates for the scaling and rotation parameters often oscillate due to a poorly conditioned learning rate ratio, addressing this by rescaling the scaling gradient with the inverse of the current scale. [ABSGS](#6127-absgs.md) [S4, unofficial] tackles the problem of fine detail recovery that is smoothed out during optimization by comparing the reconstructed image against the ground truth with a high-pass filter and back-propagating only the high-frequency residuals.
